stem: The "Valley of Death" in the automotive industry refers to:

options.A: The decline of internal combustion engine sales.
options.B: The period of negative cash flow between capital investment and volume production.
options.C: The failure rate of Tier 2 suppliers during a recession.
options.D: The gap between announcing a model and delivering it to customers.

stem: According to Porter’s Five Forces, which factor historically protected GM and Ford from new entrants?

options.B: Low capital intensity of manufacturing.
options.C: High barriers to entry due to dealer networks and capital costs.

stem: Step 2 of Musk’s "Secret Master Plan" was specifically to:

options.A: Build a high-volume car to fund a low-volume car.
options.B: Use money from the sports car to build an affordable car.
options.C: Acquire a solar energy company immediately.

stem: Tesla’s acquisition of SolarCity in 2016 is best described strategically as:

options.A: Horizontal integration to capture competitor market share.
options.B: Vertical integration to secure battery supply.
options.C: Ecosystem integration aligning with Step 4 of the Master Plan.
options.D: Unrelated diversification to hedge against auto cyclicality.

stem: In 2017, Tesla’s Gross Margin was approximately 18.9%, while Ford’s was ~10.6%. This indicates:

options.A: Tesla had lower SG&A costs than Ford.
options.B: Tesla had better unit economics but lacked sufficient scale to cover fixed costs.
options.C: Ford was pricing its vehicles aggressively to gain market share.
options.D: Tesla’s "Production Hell" had no impact on financial metrics.

stem: The "Alien Dreadnought" concept failed primarily because:

options.A: Robots were too expensive to purchase.
options.B: It underestimated the value of human flexibility in undefined processes.
options.C: The factory lacked sufficient electricity supply.
options.D: Suppliers refused to integrate with the automated system.

stem: Which structural barrier did Tesla bypass by selling directly to consumers?

options.B: NHTSA safety standards.

stem: The primary strategic risk of Tesla’s 2018 "Production Hell" was:

options.A: Brand dilution due to high volume.
options.B: Insolvency due to cash burn exceeding capital reserves.
options.C: Loss of intellectual property to Chinese competitors.

stem: Tesla’s decision to build the Gigafactory was a response to:

options.A: A desire to move manufacturing out of California.
options.B: Global supply constraints on lithium-ion batteries.
options.C: Tax incentives offered by the state of Texas exclusively.
options.D: The need to manufacture tires in-house.

stem: In the context of Disruption Theory, Tesla entered the market at the:

options.B: High end, competing on performance and design.
options.D: Commercial sector, competing on fleet costs.

stem: The "Flufferbot" anecdote illustrates a failure in:

options.B: Process Engineering and Automation Strategy.

stem: Tesla’s P/E ratio being significantly higher than GM’s implies investors view it as:

options.A: A mature value stock with stable dividends.
options.B: A distressed asset with liquidation value.

stem: Which force was NOT a significant barrier to entry for Tesla in 2004?

options.B: Access to software talent.

stem: The "Tent" (GA4) represented a shift from:

options.B: Automated rigidity to manual agility.

stem: Musk’s strategy to "burn the boats" (commit fully) is best exemplified by:

options.B: Diversifying into SpaceX and Boring Company.

stem: The "Flufferbot" was designed to perform which task?

options.B: Place fiberglass sound-deadening mats on battery packs.

stem: Tesla’s "GA4" assembly line was unique because it was:

options.A: Fully automated with no human workers.
options.B: Located in a temporary sprung structure (tent).

stem: Why did Tesla bring seat manufacturing in-house for the Model X?

options.A: To lower costs by using cheaper materials.
options.B: Because external suppliers failed to deliver the complex "monopost" design.
options.D: To increase the weight of the vehicle.

stem: Musk admitted that "excessive automation" was a mistake because:

options.A: Robots were too slow compared to humans.
options.B: Humans are better at dealing with unexpected variances and anomalies.
options.C: The electricity costs were too high.
options.D: The robots were hacking the software.

stem: A traditional automotive OEM typically outsources what percentage of the vehicle value?
The "Alien Dreadnought" concept aimed to maximize:

options.B: Volumetric velocity (speed of the line).

stem: In 2018, Tesla’s primary operational bottleneck was in:

options.B: General Assembly of the Model 3.

stem: The "Monopost" seat design in the Model X was difficult because:

options.A: It required a single pedestal rather than rails, demanding tight tolerances.
options.B: It used leather that was illegal in California.
options.C: It was too light for safety regulations.
options.D: It blocked the driver's rear view.

stem: Which manufacturing metric was critical for Tesla to achieve profitability in Q3 2018?

options.B: 2,500 cars/week.

stem: Vertical integration of battery production (Gigafactory) allows Tesla to:

options.B: Control the cell chemistry and reduce supply chain dependency.

stem: Unlike ICE vehicles, an electric vehicle powertrain typically has:

options.B: A complex multi-gear transmission.
options.C: Fewer moving parts (~20) and a single-speed transmission.

stem: The "Sprung structure" (Tent) took approximately how long to build?

options.B: 6 months.

stem: Tesla’s approach to "beta testing" the Model 3 production line was:

options.B: Skipped entirely to save time ("building the airplane while flying").

stem: Which component did Tesla notoriously struggle to weld during the Model 3 ramp?

options.B: The steel body-in-white.

stem: The operational lesson from the "Tent" experience was:

options.B: Agility and crude improvisation can beat rigid automation in a crisis.
options.C: Factories must be beautiful to be efficient.
options.D: Weather conditions do not affect manufacturing.

stem: In Q1 2018, Tesla’s operating income was approximately:

options.B: Break-even.

stem: Tesla’s "Cash Burn" is calculated as:

options.B: Cash flow from operations - Capital Expenditures (CapEx).

stem: In 2017, Tesla’s R&D intensity (R&D as % of Revenue) was roughly:

options.B: 5% (similar to GM).

stem: Despite massive losses in 2017, Tesla’s Gross Margin was:

options.B: Higher than GM's and Ford's.

stem: The dramatic turnaround in Q3 2018 profitability was driven by:

options.B: Selling Bitcoin.
options.C: Operating leverage from hitting the 5,000/week volume target.

stem: Why is the automotive industry considered to have "High Operating Leverage"?

options.A: Variable costs are high, fixed costs are low.
options.B: High fixed costs mean small volume increases lead to large profit jumps once breakeven is passed.
options.C: It relies heavily on debt financing.
options.D: Labor unions control the cost structure.

stem: In Q1 2018, Tesla’s cash balance was ~$2.7 billion and quarterly burn was ~$1 billion. This implied:

options.A: A runway of less than 3 quarters.
options.B: Infinite runway.

stem: The "Founder's Premium" in Tesla’s stock price refers to:

options.A: The salary paid to Elon Musk.
options.B: The extra valuation investors assign due to belief in Musk’s vision.
options.C: The cost of insurance for the CEO.

stem: How did Tesla generate revenue from competitors?

options.B: Selling ZEV (Zero Emission Vehicle) regulatory credits.

stem: Compared to GM, Tesla’s 2017 inventory turnover was likely:

options.A: Much faster due to direct sales.
options.B: Slower due to "production hell" bottlenecks.

stem: CapEx (Capital Expenditure) in 2017-2018 was primarily directed toward:

options.B: Dividend payments.
options.C: Model 3 production capacity and Gigafactory construction.

stem: If Tesla were valued as a traditional car company (P/E ~6), its stock price in 2018 would have:

options.B: Collapsed by >80%.

stem: Solvency risk refers to:

options.A: The inability to meet long-term financial obligations.
options.B: A temporary dip in stock price.

stem: Tesla’s negative working capital cycle (collecting cash before paying suppliers) is:

options.B: A source of interest-free financing from suppliers.

stem: The 2018 compensation package for Elon Musk was entirely:

options.B: Cash bonus-based.

stem: The "Funding Secured" tweet in August 2018 resulted in:

options.B: A $40 million SEC settlement and Musk stepping down as Chairman.
options.D: The acquisition of Tesla by the Saudi PIF.

stem: In 2024, Musk threatened to build AI products outside Tesla unless:

options.A: He was paid a cash bonus.
options.B: He was granted ~25% voting control.

stem: The primary criticism of the SolarCity acquisition was:

options.B: It was a "bailout" of a family-owned company with poor financials.
options.D: The technology was too advanced for Tesla.

stem: Musk’s decision to sleep on the factory floor is an example of:

options.B: Extreme commitment signaling, but potential failure of delegation.
options.C: Standard CEO behavior in the auto industry.

stem: Proxy advisors (ISS, Glass Lewis) recommended voting AGAINST the 2018 pay package because:

options.B: Musk already owned ~20% of the company and was sufficiently incentivized.

stem: "Key Man Risk" at Tesla refers to:

options.A: The reliance on the Chief Designer.
options.B: The existential dependence on Elon Musk’s brand and vision.
options.C: The risk of losing the head of HR.
options.D: The reliance on a single robot supplier.

stem: The board’s role in the "Funding Secured" incident was criticized for:

options.A: Being too aggressive with the SEC.
options.B: Lack of independent oversight and control over the CEO’s communications.

stem: Tesla’s board composition in 2018 was criticized for lacking:

options.A: Independence (many members had close ties to Musk).
options.B: Technical expertise.

stem: Musk’s dual role as CEO of Tesla and SpaceX creates:

options.B: Conflicts of interest regarding time allocation and resource focus.

stem: A "Dual-Class Share Structure" (which Tesla does not have, but Musk desires via options) allows:

options.A: Founders to maintain voting control with minority economic ownership.
options.B: Shareholders to vote twice.
options.D: Employees to set their own wages.

stem: The Delaware court voided Musk’s 2018 pay package in 2024 because:

options.A: Tesla failed to hit the targets.
options.B: The process was flawed and the board was not independent.

stem: Governance at Tesla is often described as a trade-off between:

options.B: Traditional oversight and Visionary speed/innovation.

stem: The 2018 SEC settlement required Tesla to add:

options.B: A new CEO.
options.D: A compliance officer from the SEC.

stem: Musk’s request for 25% voting control in 2024 was triggered by his desire to:

options.B: Control the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics.

stem: The "Technoking" title adopted by Musk in 2021 signals:

options.A: A formal change in corporate bylaws.
options.B: A disregard for traditional corporate norms and titles.
